## MAC-015 — Compact source map

**Source:** OECD, *OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022* (Feb. 2022). International-organization policy synthesis; committee review occurred **22 Nov. 2021**, with approval **10 Dec. 2021** (p.5). Most findings are OECD analysis, projections, or recommendations—not proof of enactment or AMLO-attributable outcomes.

### Atomic claims

- **Observed/reported fact — shock response (5B.9):** Mexico increased health expenditure by **0.4% of GDP in 2020**; measures also included front-loaded old-age pension payments by **8 months**, loans to qualifying SMEs/domestic and independent workers, development-bank liquidity support and guarantees, and a **three-month** mortgage subsidy for eligible displaced workers. Monetary authorities cut rates by **300 basis points, Mar. 2020–Feb. 2021**; central-bank financial-system measures amounted to **up to 3.5% of GDP**. **Locator:** p.20, Box 1.1. **Source basis:** “COVID Policy tracker database”; implementation details require primary-source verification.

- **OECD comparative finding — fiscal response (5B.9):** The initial fiscal response was among the lowest in emerging markets. Public spending increased by **around 0.7% of GDP**, versus **4.4% of GDP in emerging economies**; within programmable spending, social protection and health rose by **0.7 and 0.4 percentage points**, respectively, in **2020 relative to 2019**. **Locator:** pp.25–26, “Macroeconomic policies…” continuing onto p.26; Figure 1.11 uses estimates as of **27 Sept. 2021**.

- **Observed fact plus OECD interpretation — fiscal/debt path (5B.3):** Revenues rose marginally despite the activity contraction; the OECD attributes resilience to tax-code changes, stronger pursuit of pending liabilities, stabilization funds, and an oil hedge. The **official** public-debt measure rose from **44% at end-2019 to 55% of GDP at end-2020**, attributed to the deficit, peso depreciation, and GDP contraction. **Locator:** p.26, “Gaining fiscal space…” **Qualification:** authorial causal synthesis; underlying official series should be checked.

- **Official figures/forecasts — fiscal aggregates (5B.3):** SHCP data report public-sector borrowing requirements of **−4.0% of GDP in 2020**, **−3.8% in 2021**, and forecasts of **−3.5% in 2022**, **−3.2% in 2023**, **−2.9% in 2024**; net public-sector debt is shown at **51.5%, 49.9%, 49.7%, 49.5%, and 49.4%**, respectively. **Locator:** p.28, Table 1.4. **Qualification:** 2022–24 marked forecasts; rows may not sum because of rounding.

- **OECD scenario, not outcome (5B.3/5B.10):** Debt stabilization depends on assumptions including OECD 2021–23 growth/inflation projections, convergence to **3% inflation**, a constant peso–dollar exchange rate, specified primary balances, and later ageing costs. A downside scenario imposes a one-off **10% exchange-rate shock** and permanent **100-basis-point** yield-curve increase. **Locator:** p.29, Figure 1.13 note.

- **OECD assessment/recommendation — fiscal institutions (5B.3/5B.7):** The current-spending rule covers only **around 36% of public-sector expenditure**; OECD recommends a long-term debt anchor, wider spending-rule coverage, and an independent, adequately resourced fiscal council. **Locator:** p.14, “Further improving macroeconomic policies.” Table 1.5 records **“No action taken”** on the fiscal-council recommendation. **Locator:** p.30, Table 1.5.

- **Observed and projected macro data (5B.10):** Real GDP changed **−8.2% in 2020** and **+5.3% in 2021**; OECD projected **+2.3% in 2022** and **+2.6% in 2023**. CPI inflation was projected at **5.6% in 2022** and **3.4% in 2023**. **Locator:** p.22, Table 1.2. **Do not treat projections as realized results.**

- **OECD/central-bank-based assessment — financial resilience (5B.3):** Banks had capital and liquidity above regulatory minima and contained non-performing loans, but loan deterioration remained possible after 2020 forbearance ended. Banxico stress tests suggested system-wide buffers could withstand extreme events; smaller and medium banks exposed to SMEs and consumer credit could still be substantially affected. **Locator:** p.23, first paragraph. **Contrary/risk material:** resilience is qualified, not unconditional.

- **OECD interpretation — investment and regulation (5B.4):** Investment was muted since **2015** and falling since **2019**; OECD says domestic-policy uncertainty, especially electricity-market reform proposals, hindered investment. It recommends certainty for existing contracts and regulatory stability. **Locator:** p.12, “Restarting investment…” **Attribution limit:** no quantified causal effect and no ruler-specific attribution.

- **OECD findings — distribution and labor (5B.8):** Informal workers, women, and youth were particularly harmed by the pandemic (p.11). Unemployment was **3.9%**, but rose to **15%** when including people outside the labor force who would accept work, and **24%** when adding underemployment; women’s participation recovered more slowly. **Locator:** p.21, opening paragraph and Figure 1.6 note.

- **OECD modelled interpretation (5B.4/5B.8/5B.10):** A combined reform scenario is estimated to raise GDP per capita by **25.2% over ten years**. Components rely on closing specified gaps with OECD averages; corruption closes only half the gap. OECD explicitly calls estimates **illustrative** and uncertain in magnitude and timing. **Locator:** pp.16–18, text preceding and Table 1.1 with note.

- **Observed reform record (secondary 5B.1/5B.7):** Table 1.5 reports digital services supplied from abroad became subject to VAT; a cadastral platform was being created and legal adjustments were under Senate discussion; it records no action on progressive-income-tax and intergovernmental-responsibility recommendations. **Locator:** p.30, Table 1.5. **Status caveat:** “being created/discussed” is not completion or enactment.

### Limitations and reopen list

Extract ends at p.30 and omits detailed later sections on monetary policy, competition, procurement/corruption, social programs, education, and finance. Reopen **Tables 1.9–1.13; Figures 1.21–1.40; Chapter 2**. Verify fiscal and tax claims against SHCP/SAT, monetary and stress-test claims against Banxico, and reform status against complete legal texts, amendments, effective dates, regulations, and execution records. No unresolved allegation in this extract is adjudicated; policy uncertainty and corruption references are OECD assessments, not legal findings.
